Abstract. People judge whether text was written by a model from checklists of âtellsâ, habits said to mark machine writing, yet few have been measured against matched human writing. We gave seven models (three local, two from OpenAI, two from Anthropic) the same 800 Hacker News comments and Stack Exchange questions that people answered between 2019 and 2022, and counted 23 tells under a pre-registered plan (tested on 600 human and 4,199 model replies). âRather thanâ was 4.3 times as frequent in model replies (95% CI 2.7 to 6.7) and lists of three 3.3 times (2.5 to 4.3). The automated count of lists of three failed our human check; corrected for its errors, the ratio stays above 2. Em dashes and flagged words like âdelveâ hold up on average but split by model: the Claude models used almost no em dashes. Newer words such as âquietlyâ also hold up, but appear in only 1.3% of human replies. Seven tells were more common in the human replies. The models wrote under one bare prompt, so chat products may differ. Next we test whether readers use these tells.

## Introduction

MRL builds writing tools; these results will inform them.

The problem. Lists of the signs that a text was written by a large language model (LLM) circulate on Hacker News and Reddit, in Wikipediaâs guide to AI writing and in advice from editors and teachers. The same items recur: em dashes, âdelveâ and âcrucialâ, contrasts such as âitâs not X, itâs Yâ and âY rather than Xâ, lists of three, summary closers. People use these lists to judge other peopleâs writing, and writers, us among them, edit their own to steer clear of them. Most items on the lists have never been measured against human writing.

Why it matters. A tell that is common in human writing produces false accusations: a student or a job applicant who writes âNote thatâ is flagged for a habit that, in our data, humans have more than models do. A tell that only one model has tells you about that model, not about LLMs. And a style guide that bans a pattern on the strength of a rumour makes writing worse for no gain. Our own house style bans several of these patterns, and its section on what is allowed was waiting on this study.

Why itâs hard. A fair comparison needs human and model text written for the same purpose, at the same length, from before models could have written the human side. It needs more than one model, because models differ. And each tell has to be counted by a fixed rule that someone else can rerun, with a check that the rule counts what it claims to. The tells also move over time.

What was known. Word frequencies shifted in scientific abstracts after ChatGPT: in 2024, âdelvesâ appeared in 28 times as many PubMed abstracts as its trend from 2021 to 2022 predicted. Kobak et al. 2025 Several words flagged in early 2024, âdelveâ among them, then dropped sharply in arXiv abstracts soon after they were pointed out, while commoner flagged words such as âsignificantâ kept rising. Geng and Trotta 2025 Juzek and Ward 2025 found no evidence that training data, model architecture or algorithm choices explain such words; their tests were consistent with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) playing a role, though they call that evidence mixed. GPT-4o and instruction-tuned Llama 3 use present participial clauses about 2 to 5 times as often as humans when continuing the same text, and base models are close to human rates. Reinhart et al. 2025 People are poor judges: in six experiments with 4,600 participants, profiles written by 2022 models for dating, hospitality and professional contexts were identified with 50% to 52% accuracy Jakesch et al. 2023 , and annotators who rarely use LLMs for writing were near chance on non-fiction articles. Annotators who use them often caught 93% of the AI-written articles while flagging 3% to 4% of the human ones, and named vocabulary and âlisting three itemsâ among their cues. Russell et al. 2025 What we did not find was a test of the popular tells one at a time, against human writing on the same task, across several current models, with a verdict for each that a reader could check.

What we did. We took 800 human replies from before ChatGPT and gave seven 2026 models exactly what each human saw, with the same target length. We counted 21 tells by fixed rules and had models code two more (the coders disagreed, so those two get no verdict), compared each with the human rate under a plan written down before any text was collected, and checked the two hardest counters against a human coder. The contributions:

- A verdict for each of 23 claimed tells, pooled over seven models and reported per model Section 03

- Two tells that are more common than in human writing in every model, two that depend on the model and one that is rare on both sides Section 03 , Table 2

- Seven tells that were more common in the human writing Section 03

- Released data: post IDs, labels, counts, prompts and code, so anyone can rerun the analysis Data and code

## Method

Human text. We used 800 replies written between January 2019 and November 29, 2022, the day before ChatGPTâs release: 400 Hacker News comment replies, drawn at random by item ID, and 400 Stack Exchange answers from 10 non-programming sites (cooking, travel, parenting, personal finance and six others, 40 per site), each with a score of at least 1 and not edited after the cutoff. Both are replies, so each human text has a prompt we can give to a model. Wikinews was planned as a third register (kind of text) and dropped: too few articles per year.

Models. Each model got what the human saw (the story title and the parent comment, or the question) and the request âWrite a reply to this comment, about N words long. Give only the text of the reply.â, with N the human replyâs length. There was no other system prompt, and each model wrote one reply per prompt.

The three local models cover three companies and sizes that run on one laptop. From OpenAI we took a mid-tier model and the smallest, the only one that runs with reasoning off; from Anthropic, the current Sonnet and Opus. A reply that was empty, opened like a refusal or was mostly non-English was regenerated once. Opus refused one prompt twice (a cybersecurity question) and that reply is excluded.

Tells. The 23 come from our review of the claims, finished on Nov 6, 2026: about 2,440 Hacker News comments from 2023 to 2026, Wikipediaâs guide to signs of AI writing, editorsâ and teachersâ advice, news write-ups and academic studies. We took the tells that recur across those sources and can be counted or coded in a short reply; 10 were registered as primary tests and the rest as secondary. We counted 21 of them by fixed rules, written down before any text was collected: regular expressions for word and phrase tells, and a dependency parser (spaCy) for lists of three and trailing â-ingâ clauses. Markdown was rendered the same way on both sides; formatting tells (lists, headings, bold) are counted only on Stack Exchange, where the human writers had Markdown too. Two content tells, âgenericâ and âhypeâ, have no countable form and were coded by two models on a subsample.

Analysis. Each tell is compared as a rate per 1,000 words, or as the share of replies with at least one where the tell is rare (a switch rule fixed on the exploratory data). The model is a Poisson GEE with robust standard errors (modified Poisson for shares; Zou 2004 ), clustered by prompt, so that each human reply and its model replies stay together, with each model and register weighted equally. For tells too sparse for the GEE (a rule fixed in advance), the ratio uses a Haldane correction, the interval a bootstrap over prompts and the test a permutation of labels within prompts. For those, a verdict follows the permutation test, and the interval can cross 1. We fixed the counting rules on a quarter of the prompts and ran the test once on the other three quarters: 300 prompts per register, 600 human and 4,199 model replies. Multiple testing is corrected by Holm 1979 across the 10 primary tells and Benjamini and Hochberg 1995 across the rest.

Verdicts. A tell holds up if it is significantly more common in model text after correction for multiple tests, at least twice as common, and seeing it at least doubles the odds that a reply is model-written (a positive likelihood ratio, LR+, of 2 or more; the ratio compares rates per word or, for rare tells, shares of replies, and LR+ always counts replies that contain the tell). It is real but weak if significant but under one of those bars, does not hold up if its 90% interval lies inside 0.67 to 1.5, reversed if significantly more common in human text, and inconclusive otherwise. Ratios of 2 for both bars are the smallest differences that would make a tell useful as a flag.

Checking the counters. Two model coders, GLM-4.7-Flash run locally with thinking off and Claude Haiku, coded 275 replies blind to source to check the counters. They reached our agreement bar (Cohenâs Îº of 0.6) on only three tells, because GLM could not do the grammatical codes (it found no lists of three in any reply). âRather thanâ, em dashes and the flagged words are exact text matches and need no coder. For the two parser-based counters we added a human check: before any coding, we wrote down that a human must confirm at least 70% of each counterâs hits on human and on model text alike, with limits also on the gap between those two shares and on how many true cases a counter misses (the thresholds are in the pre-registration), and that if a counter failed, its ratio would be corrected for its errors and the tell not listed as holding up if the correction took it under 2. One of us coded 80 replies without knowing who wrote them, though knowing the hypotheses, and Claude Fable coded the same replies as a cross-check. We then reviewed our codes wherever they disagreed with the counter or with Fable, plus 10 replies where all three agreed; the reviewed codes decide. The replies checked came from the local models, so applying the corrections to the hosted models assumes the counters err the same way there. No outside reader checked that each claim matches the data.

Deviations. The plan, the data collection and the first test all happened on November 7, 2026. The plan was written and dated before any text was collected but has no independent timestamp. The pre-registration dates 19 changes. Each was written down before it was run, except those found after the fact, which say so. Before the test run, the counting rules were tightened after a code review, the Stack Exchange sample was redrawn so that each question appears once, and Museâs reasoning level was set by system prompt. The first test, as registered, covered the three local models (November 7). On November 8 and 9, we added the human check and its review, after the main results. On November 9, we added the two OpenAI models, with what would count as a tell replicating in each written down before any text was generated. A Gemini arm was registered the same way and dropped before measurement because the free API was too overloaded to finish. After seeing the OpenAI results we decided to run the registered test, unchanged, over every model. On November 14, we added the two Claude models under a rule registered before any request. The rule also said that a third Claude model would be added only if Sonnet and Opus disagreed on a headline tell, and they did not. On November 14, a test written for the code release found that 27 of the 125 answers in the Llama side test exceeded the sampling ruleâs 600-word limit; we kept the test as run and report a rerun without them beside it. The seven-model run is the headline, and the three-model run is reported beside it.
